cards.explanation: The answer is False. The Teacher says "Everything is futile!" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). He doesn't say some things or a few things. He says everything, and he opens with "Futility of futilities…" It's a big opening line, friends, and it sets up everything else he looks at.

The answer is what a man gains from it. The Teacher asks, "What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun?" (Ecclesiastes 1:3). He's looking at the pile of work and asking what comes out the other end. I've asked myself that after a long day at the ovens, friends, usually while scraping dough off my hat.

The answer is remains. The Teacher says, "Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever." (Ecclesiastes 1:4). People come and go, and the earth remains. It's like a batch of cookies, friends: a whole crowd shows up, the plate empties, everybody leaves, and the plate is still sitting there.

The answer is that it hurries back to where it rises. The Teacher says the sun "…hurries back to where it rises." (Ecclesiastes 1:5). It sets, and then it's already rushing back to start again. No lunch break, no nap, just straight back to the beginning. I know that kind of schedule, friends.

The answer is returning on its course. The Teacher says the wind swirls "round and round…" "…ever returning on its course." (Ecclesiastes 1:6). South, then north, then around again. If I followed that wind, friends, I'd end up right back at my own oven door.

The answer is True. The Teacher says, "All the rivers flow into the sea, yet the sea is never full…" (Ecclesiastes 1:7). Every river keeps pouring in and the sea still has room. I wish my cookie boxes worked like that, friends. Actually, I take that back, I'd never get to rest.

The answer is back to the place they came from. The Teacher says, "to the place from which the streams come, there again they flow." (Ecclesiastes 1:7). The water goes right back to where it started, and then it all begins again. That's a commute with no weekend, friends, and I thought my old drawer days were repetitive.

The answer is that they never get enough. The Teacher says, "the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing." (Ecclesiastes 1:8). You can look and listen all day, and they still want more. It's like scrolling your phone at midnight, saying "just one more," and somehow it's 2 a.m.

The answer is new. The Teacher says, "there is nothing new under the sun." (Ecclesiastes 1:9). What has been will be again, and what has been done will be done again. It's like getting a "brand new" idea in the shower, friends, and then finding out you had the same one last year.

The answer is False. The Teacher says, "…those yet to come will not be remembered by those who follow after." (Ecclesiastes 1:11). He says no remembrance, not for those who came before and not for those yet to come. It's a heavy line, friends, and he doesn't soften it.
